title: The Broad Street Pump
subtitle: A doctor with a map, an outbreak nobody could explain, and the beginning of a science.
description: A B2 reading and listening text on John Snow's investigation of the 1854 cholera outbreak in London, with past-tense practice and comprehension exercises.
passage: John Snow was born in York in 1813, the eldest of nine children in a family with no money to speak of. At fourteen he was apprenticed to a surgeon, which was how medicine was entered at the time, and he went on to qualify in London. He became one of the best anaesthetists in the country — he gave chloroform to Queen Victoria at two of her births — and that is not what he is remembered for.

In the summer of 1854, cholera broke out in Soho, in central London. It killed with a speed that is hard to convey: a person could be well in the morning and dead before the next morning. In the worst week, more than five hundred people died within a few streets.

Nobody knew how the disease travelled. The accepted explanation was miasma — bad air rising from filth and standing water — and it was not a stupid theory. It fitted the observation that outbreaks were worst in the poorest and dirtiest districts, and it was held by almost every serious authority in the country. Snow thought it was wrong. He had argued for years that cholera was swallowed rather than breathed, mainly because it attacked the gut first, which is not what an airborne poison would do.

What he did about it was the part that mattered. He went into the affected streets and recorded every death he could trace — where the person lived, and where their household drew its water. Then he drew a map, marking each death as a bar at its address. The pattern was not subtle once it was on paper. The deaths clustered around a single public water pump in Broad Street, and they thinned out with distance from it.

The anomalies were what made the case. A workhouse in the middle of the cluster, with over five hundred inmates, had almost no deaths — it had its own well. A brewery nearby lost none of its workers; the men drank beer, and the brewery too had its own supply. And a widow in Hampstead, miles away, died of cholera for no visible reason, until it emerged that she had liked the taste of Broad Street water and had it delivered by cart. Each of those cases would have looked like a problem for the theory. Each of them, examined, confirmed it.

Snow took his evidence to the parish authorities and persuaded them to remove the handle from the pump. The outbreak was already declining by then, and honest historians say the removal probably did not end it. That does not diminish what happened, because the argument was never really about one pump. Later investigation found the pump's well had been dug within a metre of an old cesspit, and that a nappy from a baby with cholera had been washed into it.

The Board of Health rejected his explanation. Their report concluded that the evidence pointed to the air, and Snow died in 1858 without seeing his theory accepted. The germ theory that would have explained his findings was still two decades away.

What survives is not really the conclusion but the method: define the population, count the cases, map them against a suspected cause, and then hunt for the cases that do not fit. That is epidemiology, and it was assembled in a few weeks in Soho by a man who was, on the only point that mattered, alone.

images.alt: A hand-coloured caricature of a woman recoiling as she looks at a drop of water through a magnifying glass, full of monstrous creatures
images.caption: “Monster Soup commonly called Thames Water”, William Heath, 1828. Londoners already knew the water was filthy; what nobody had established was that filthy water was what killed you.

images.alt: Snow's 1854 map of Soho, with each cholera death marked as a black bar against the building where it occurred
images.caption: Snow's own map, 1854. Each black bar is a death, stacked against the house it happened in — and the bars pile up around the pump in Broad Street.

exercises.title: Past Tenses
exercises.instructions: A historical narrative uses the past simple for events, the past perfect for what came before them, and the past continuous for what was going on around them.

items.prompt: John Snow ___ born in York in 1813 and ___ the eldest of nine children.
items.explanation: A stated past date takes the past simple throughout.

items.prompt: When he ___ fourteen, he ___ working for a surgeon.
items.explanation: “When he was fourteen” places both verbs in finished past time.

items.prompt: In 1854 people ___ dying in Soho and nobody ___ why.
items.explanation: Know is a state verb and never takes the continuous, in any tense.

items.prompt: He discovered that the people who ___ all ___ the same water.
items.explanation: Both are finished events inside the same past narrative.

items.prompt: The well ___ ___ within a metre of an old cesspit, which nobody realised at the time.
items.explanation: Past perfect passive: the digging happened before the outbreak, which is the point of using it.

items.prompt: The outbreak ___ already ___ when the handle was removed.
items.explanation: Past continuous for something in progress at the moment of another past event.

exercises.title: Understanding the Investigation
exercises.instructions: Read for the method, which is what the text says actually survives.

items.prompt: Why does the writer say the miasma theory “was not a stupid theory”?
options: It fitted the observation that outbreaks were worst in the poorest, dirtiest districts
It had been proved in other countries
It explained why cholera attacked the gut
items.explanation: The text is careful to make the wrong theory reasonable before showing why it failed — which is what makes Snow's dissent impressive rather than obvious.

items.prompt: What was Snow's argument for cholera being swallowed?
options: It attacked the gut first, which an airborne poison would not do
It affected only people who drank from pumps
items.explanation: A reasoning from symptoms, years before he had the Soho data.

options: The route of the water pipes under Soho
Which households had refused to move
Deaths clustered around one pump and thinning out with distance from it
items.explanation: “The pattern was not subtle once it was on paper” — the map is what made an invisible pattern visible.

items.prompt: Why were the workhouse and the brewery important?
options: They were the first places the disease appeared
They sat inside the cluster yet had almost no deaths — and each had its own water supply
They refused to let Snow collect data
items.explanation: “Each of those cases would have looked like a problem for the theory. Each of them, examined, confirmed it.”

items.prompt: Why did the widow in Hampstead die?
options: She had visited Soho during the outbreak
She had liked the taste of Broad Street water and had it delivered
items.explanation: A death miles from the cluster that turns out to confirm rather than contradict it.

items.prompt: How does the writer treat the removal of the pump handle?
options: As the moment the outbreak ended
As a mistake that cost lives
As probably not what ended the outbreak, which does not diminish the argument
items.explanation: “The argument was never really about one pump” — the writer refuses the neat version of the story.

items.prompt: What does the writer say actually survives from Snow's work?
options: The method: define the population, count, map, and hunt for the cases that do not fit
The conclusion that water carries cholera
items.explanation: “That is epidemiology” — and the final clause notes he was alone on the point that mattered.

exercises.title: True or False?
exercises.instructions: Decide whether each statement matches the text.

items.statement: Snow is best remembered for his work as an anaesthetist.
items.explanation: False — he was one of the best in the country, “and that is not what he is remembered for”.

items.statement: The miasma theory was a minority view at the time.
items.explanation: False — it “was held by almost every serious authority in the country”. Snow was the minority.

items.statement: The brewery workers avoided cholera partly because they drank beer.
items.explanation: True — and the brewery also had its own water supply.
False — the Board of Health rejected it and concluded the evidence pointed to the air.

items.statement: Snow lived to see his theory accepted.
items.explanation: False — he died in 1858, and germ theory was still about twenty years away.

discussion: Snow was right and could not prove why, because the mechanism had not been discovered. How should experts treat a conclusion that works without an explanation?
The anomalies — the workhouse, the brewery, the widow — turned out to be the strongest evidence. Why is the case that does not fit so valuable?
The Board of Health rejected the evidence and was wrong. What makes an established consensus hard to shift?
“The argument was never really about one pump.” Why do neat stories attach themselves to complicated discoveries?
Write about 200 words describing a problem you would investigate by counting and mapping rather than by reasoning about it.
